item.title: Election 'human error' delays key primary results in latest voting mishap to hit blue states
item.description: David Crowley's narrow win over Francesca Hong was delayed 90 minutes after five USB flash drives failed to download Milwaukee election data.
item.content:encoded:
Milwaukee's election results from Tuesday's primary were delayed because of a "human error" in which five of the nine USB flash drives did not download the election results, prompting critics to call it a showing of "complete incompetence."

The error effectively stalled the results of the closely watched Democratic gubernatorial primary between Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Francesca Hong. The delay came amid heightened scrutiny of election administration in Democratic-led jurisdictions, where recent ballot and reporting errors have drawn criticism and, in some cases, investigations from Republican lawmakers.

"We’re all human, and humans can make errors," Paulina Gutiérrez, executive director of the Milwaukee Election Commission, said during a midnight news conference.

The error delayed the county's election results by an hour as Gutiérrez and Milwaukee Election Commission staffers returned to Central Count with a police escort to retrieve the remaining voting data.

HASAN PIKER WARNS ‘THE KNIVES WILL BE OUT’ AFTER SOCIALIST FRANCESCA HONG FALLS IN WISCONSIN UPSET

"So basically what we need to do is go back to the operations center and we're going to download out five of those machines the results and make sure that's not the audit log," Gutiérrez said during the press conference "So have the reports printed from the first download. We're going to reprint and start the process so that can compare those results."

The Milwaukee Election Commission said in a news release that the audit log, which documents activity on the tabulator, was downloaded rather than the election results.

"The issue delayed the reporting of Milwaukee's results, but it did not affect the results," the press release stated. "The election results remained intact and unchanged on the tabulators. No ballots were lost or changed, or needed to be recounted or retabulated."

Gutiérrez said there were no issues with the voting machines themselves but confirmed to a reporter that a wrong button was pushed in downloading the data.

In an interview with Votebeat, Gutiérrez said the time it took to download results from the tabulators varied. She said that while the standard time frame was 10 minutes, some tabulators completed the downloads in three minutes.

MARYLAND BALLOT BLUNDER SPARKS HOUSE GOP PROBE AHEAD OF PRIMARY

"The fact that this happened five times seems more like a training issue," former Milwaukee Election Commissioner Claire Woodall told Votebeat. "Was this person trained on how to export results? Are they familiar with the machines and how you export results?"

The error meant that 15,000 votes had yet to be counted at that point.

NBC News' Steve Kornacki buried his face in his hand after learning of Milwaukee's error on live TV.

"We’re kind of indefinitely waiting for them to get their act together here," Kornacki said. "We waited 90 minutes for them. They did this whole procession, and then we find out there’s nothing on the sticks."

HOUSE PANEL DEMANDS CLASSIFIED BRIEFINGS ON NONCITIZEN VOTING, ALLEGED CHINESE ELECTION INTERFERENCE

After the remaining election data was properly downloaded after 1 a.m., Milwaukee County Clerk George Christenson addressed reporters and emphasized the importance of being transparent with the public.

"At the end of the day, what’s important is that we’re transparent, that the results are secure, and that we’re open and honest ," Christenson said, "And that’s what the City of Milwaukee election director did. She came up here and she explained it, went back, got the results, brought it back to us, and we got everything right."

But despite the transparency, critics did not hold back.

"Complete incompetence at the facility isn’t helping anything here," Republican state Rep. Scott Krug wrote on X. "This was human error that could have easily been double checked before leaving the facility. More than one answer to the problem not one silver bullet"

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The Milwaukee error follows other election-administration problems in various blue states. New Jersey recently disclosed that a software error improperly registered roughly 6,600 people who had indicated they were not U.S. citizens, with fewer than 400 later casting ballots. In Oregon, officials said DMV errors resulted in 1,945 people being registered without providing proof of eligibility, 44 of whom voted. And a Connecticut judge ordered a new Democratic mayoral primary in Bridgeport after finding evidence of absentee-ballot violations cast the original result into doubt.

This is also not the first "human error" involving the Milwaukee Election Commission.

During the 2024 presidential election, election officials recounted 31,000 absentee ballots because staffers did not lock tabulator doors. The error delayed results from 105,000 absentee ballots.

During the 2020 presidential election, then-Milwaukee Election Commissioner Claire Woodall left one of the 12 flash drives containing election results at Central Count, delaying the reporting of roughly 169,000 absentee ballots.

Wisconsin Election Commission spokesperson Emilee Miklas said that while errors may happen, Wisconsin's election integrity is secure.

"Wisconsin elections are safe, secure, and accurate due to multiple checks and balances. While human mistake can happen – Wisconsin’s election system, which includes layers of oversight at the local and state level, ensures things are caught and corrected," Miklas said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

The race between Crowley and Hong was officially called at 2:34 a.m. Wednesday, with Crowley winning by 0.5%.

item.title: Nicole Kidman admits she was ‘very fearful and deeply vulnerable’ after Keith Urban divorce
item.description: Nicole Kidman says her divorce from Keith Urban left her future "completely unknown," despite surviving her split from Tom Cruise decades earlier.
item.content:encoded:
Nicole Kidman has been through one highly scrutinized Hollywood divorce before — but she says splitting from Keith Urban hasn't made heartbreak any easier.

"It's all new," the actress said in a cover interview with British Vogue. "Every time!"

Just months after her 19-year marriage to Keith Urban officially ended, the Oscar-winning actress is opening up about the emotional journey of starting over — admitting there was a point when she was "very fearful and deeply vulnerable" but ultimately decided she had to move forward.

NICOLE KIDMAN FILES FOR DIVORCE FROM KEITH URBAN CITING 'MARITAL DIFFICULTIES'

"Free falling?" she asked herself, as she searched for the right words to describe this chapter of her life. "Jumping off?"

Then came the question that seemed to capture her life at the moment.

"Like, where am I going? And what’s next?"

Kidman, 59, filed for divorce from Urban, 58, last September in Nashville after nearly two decades of marriage. Their divorce was finalized in January, with irreconcilable differences cited and Kidman named the primary residential parent of their two daughters. 

The former couple agreed to make major decisions involving the girls jointly. Neither party sought spousal support, and both waived their right to appear at the divorce hearing.

NICOLE KIDMAN PLANS ON BECOMING A DEATH DOULA AS SHE ADMITS IT 'MAY SOUND A LITTLE WEIRD'

While Kidman didn't get into the details of what led to the split, she revealed what it felt like to be on the other side of a life she thought she understood.

"I’ve approached my whole life like that," she said of her "feelings first" philosophy.

"That’s just who I am. I don’t overthink things and I’m probably not that analytical. I’m far more feeling-centred and I lead with my heart. I just go, ‘OK, what do I feel here? I’ll give it a go.’ It throws people, because I think they think I’ll be far more measured and I’m not."

Kidman has never been one to let her head overrule her heart, she suggested in her interview.

"I can still approach things intellectually," she continued with a smile, "but my desire is not to be ruled by my head. I’ve always wanted to live a well-examined life, so what does that entail? Trying things, making mistakes, failing, getting back up, moving on, embracing love, staying open, keeping the heart open and the possibilities."

The "Practical Magic" star added, "But at the same time, I’m like, ‘OK, I didn’t expect this. I had a different view of what my life was going to be, but this is what it is now.’ You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s… not. You have to adjust. You adapt. The future, it’s completely unknown to me right now."

She paused and added, "Strange."

When asked whether the uncertainty was frightening, Kidman replied, "There was a point where I was very fearful and deeply vulnerable," adding, "which is exposing. And then at the same time [I'm] going, 'Well, I can either really not confront it and just curl up, or I can just go forward with an enormous amount of hope.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I know my character. I know my talent. I know who I am. If I make a mistake and it doesn’t connect, or something goes wrong in my life where it’s humiliating, it’s OK. Other people have had that and that’s OK. Take the onus off it."

But if Kidman thought her first very public divorce had prepared her for the second, she quickly learned otherwise.

The actress was famously married to Tom Cruise for more than a decade after meeting him on the set of "Days of Thunder." They married in 1990 and adopted two children, Isabella and Connor, before divorcing in 2001.

Her marriage to Cruise began when Kidman was barely into adulthood. She has previously described being swept up in the romance and largely ignoring warnings that becoming the wife of one of Hollywood's biggest stars could affect her own career.

"Yeah, I got married so young," Kidman said. "Suddenly, I was 22, 23 years old and I had this huge movie star husband, but it just seemed completely natural."

"We just fell madly in love and it was that simple," Kidman recalled.

When people warned her that marrying Cruise could overshadow her career, she didn't hesitate.

"I’m like, ‘I don’t care. I’m in love. I want to be married.’"

She remembered the people who later said, "‘See, we told you.’"

Her response was just as defiant.

"I’m like, ‘So what? I wasn’t meant to marry the man I love? Of course, I’ll throw my career away. I don’t care.’"

"But you have to remember literally, because of who I married at such a young age, I was thrust into it since I was 22."

After Cruise, she found love with Urban, the New Zealand-born singer-songwriter and guitarist. They married in 2006 and welcomed two daughters, Sunday Rose and Faith Margaret.

item.title: World War II Memorial on National Mall vandalized with pink spray paint, fountain overflowing with bubbles
item.description: Pink spray paint reading "clean hands, dirty money" was found on the World War II Memorial as U.S. Park Police launched an active investigation.
item.content:encoded:
WASHINGTON — The World War II Memorial on the National Mall was vandalized Thursday, along with a fountain that was found overflowing with bubbles, the latest incident in which prominent monuments have been targeted in the nation's capital.

U.S. Park Police were on the scene and blocked off the area.

"Clean hands, dirty money," letters in bright pink spray paint read.

WHO IS DAVID HEARN? US OLYMPIAN WHO DENIES VANDALIZING REFLECTING POOL AFTER VIRAL ARREST

The Department of the Interior called the vandalism an "utter disgrace."

"The vandalism that occurred is an utter disgrace and will not be tolerated," an agency spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Our U.S. Park Police are on the scene and the investigation is ongoing. The public should know we will find the person responsible for this disgusting act."

The agency noted that the memorial honors the armed forces and the more than 400,000 Americans who died fighting in World War II.

WATCH: TRUMP REVEALS FLASHY NEW COLOR FOR NATIONAL MALL'S REFLECTING POOL MAKEOVER

An Army veteran who arrived at the memorial told Fox News Digital she was looking forward to seeing it and was "offended" by the act of vandalism.

"It just makes me absolutely irate," Debra Mortensen said. "I was offended because people fought and died for our country, and it’s dishonoring our country and all we’ve been through."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the U.S. Park Police and the National Park Service. No information about a potential suspect was released.

In 2016, the memorial was vandalized by someone protesting the then-controversial Dakota Access Pipeline. A vandal spray-painted the North Dakota section of the memorial with the phrase "#NoDAPL."

The memorial was closed for several months earlier this year for a $4 million renovation project upgrading the fountains and lighting, FOX DC reported. It re-opened in May.

In addition to the war memorial, other monuments on the National Mall have been targeted recently. 

In June, separate red markings of "8647," a political slogan and protest symbol used against President Donald Trump, were found on the Washington Monument, and damage was reported at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

item.title: Davis Martin ejected after back-to-back wild pitches near Sal Stewart's head spark benches-clearing incident
item.description: Davis Martin was ejected after back-to-back wild pitches near Sal Stewart's head sparked a benches-clearing altercation between the White Sox and Reds.
item.content:encoded:
Chicago White Sox starting pitcher Davis Martin was ejected from Thursday’s matinee against the Cincinnati Reds after back-to-back wild pitches led to a benches-clearing altercation.

Reds Rookie of the Year frontrunner Sal Stewart, who homered in his first at-bat off Martin, was facing a 0-1 count when a pitch sailed over everyone’s head and hit the backstop.

Stewart looked at Martin immediately, but the Sox starter tapped his chest, indicating he didn’t mean for the wild pitch.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

However, Stewart took exception, and understandably so, when a 92-mph fastball came up and in on the very next pitch from Martin. If Stewart hadn’t moved quickly, the ball may have hit him right in the face. Instead, it just clipped the brim of his helmet for a hit-by-pitch.

From there, Stewart pointed the knob end of his bat at Martin, and it was clear he, at the very least, said "that’s twice." Martin was still claiming he didn’t mean to do it, but Stewart’s Reds teammates didn’t care to hear his side.

CINCINNATI REDS PITCHER RIPS 'F—ING FATA–' UMPIRE FOR GETTING IN DEFENDER'S WAY ON GROUND BALL

MLB veteran Eugenio Suarez was among those shown on the broadcast running out to say his piece to Martin. The White Sox dugout, though, was quick to move as well.

White Sox catcher Edgar Quero was pivotal in the situation not getting out of control, as he popped up from his place behind home plate and stopped Stewart from walking toward his pitcher. Quero even walked down the first base line with Stewart as the situation unfolded.

After the tension dissipated, umpires reviewed the situation to see if Martin should be tossed from the game. Considering that both pitches were near Stewart’s head, umpires eventually made the decision to toss the White Sox starter before he could complete three innings.

Stewart got the party started for the Reds at the beginning of the game, launching a home run on a hanging breaking ball by Martin into the left field seats. Some argued on social media that was the reason Martin may have been throwing those pitches intentionally, but it didn’t seem Stewart did anything extra after hitting the solo blast.

Martin also allowed a two-run homer to Suarez later in that first frame, as the Reds quickly put up three runs on the White Sox. But at the time of Martin’s ejection, Chicago had scored four runs of their own to take the lead as the top of the third got underway.

Chicago, though, was forced to bring in Erick Fedde on emergency notice and Cincinnati made him pay. The Reds scored four runs in the top of the fourth inning to take an 8-4 lead. They would go on to win the game, 9-8, holding off the White Sox, who scored three runs in the eighth and ninth innings combined.

Stewart is having himself quite the 2026 campaign, as the first-time All-Star is now hitting .259 with an .811 OPS and 26 home runs after his 2-for-3 day at the dish.

item.title: Tony Romo may have cost himself coveted CBS position after arrest, former NFL QB says
item.description: Tony Romo's arrest on suspicion of intoxicated driving may end his CBS career, says Boomer Esiason, as J.J. Watt replaces him alongside Jim Nantz.
item.content:encoded:
Tony Romo’s time in the CBS broadcast booth could soon be coming to an end, according to former NFL quarterback and sports analyst Boomer Esiason.

"If I had to guess, purely speculation given what’s going on right now, I would think it’s over," Esiason said on WFAN.

"He may end up going somewhere else and getting things straightened out."

NFL ANALYST TONY ROMO PLACED ON LEAVE BY CBS SPORTS FOLLOWING DRUNK DRIVING ARREST IN WISCONSIN

Esiason's warning comes after Romo was arrested in Milwaukee in late July on suspicion of driving while intoxicated.

Police booked the former Dallas Cowboys star after he failed field sobriety tests and refused a chemical test. And CBS reacted fast. The network placed Romo on indefinite leave and promoted J.J. Watt to replace him alongside Jim Nantz and Tracy Wolfson in the lead broadcast booth.

Esiason explained that moving Romo to another role at CBS isn't realistic. When Romo took over the top spot in 2017, CBS shipped veteran quarterback Phil Simms to The NFL Today. That escape hatch is gone. The studio desk is already packed, especially after adding Russell Wilson. And moving a $17 million broadcaster down the pecking order to call lower-profile games hardly makes sense.

That leaves CBS with one logical move: cut ties altogether.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

For CBS, the arrest could provide an easy exit from a partnership that had already lost its shine. Romo burst onto the scene in 2017 by predicting plays before they happened, but the magic has worn off. Critics and fans have hammered him for poor preparation, repetitive comments and constantly talking over Nantz. Things got bad enough that CBS executives reportedly sat Romo down in 2023 and told him to clean up his act in the booth.

CBS was already paying top dollar for diminishing returns.

Now, with a high-profile arrest right before the football season begins, the network could have a path to walk away completely. The arrest may be the final straw for CBS, but Romo had been wearing out his welcome in the booth long before police pulled him over.

item.title: Overturned cars shut down multiple 405 Freeway lanes in West Los Angeles during morning commute
item.description: California Highway Patrol closed three Los Angeles 405 Freeway lanes as crews worked to clear two overturned cars near Santa Monica Boulevard.
item.content:encoded:
Two cars overturned on Los Angeles’ 405 Freeway during the Thursday morning rush hour, closing several northbound lanes and triggering a major traffic backup.

The crash was reported shortly before 7:30 a.m. near Santa Monica Boulevard, according to the California Highway Patrol (CHP).

At least one person involved in the crash declined to be taken to a hospital, CHP reported. It was not immediately clear whether anyone suffered serious injuries.

The overturned cars blocked lanes as emergency crews responded to the scene. Video from KTLA showed traffic stacking up behind the crash as some drivers caught in the growing backup attempted to exit the freeway.

HUNDREDS BLOCK FLORIDA INTERSTATE IN ALLEGED STREET TAKEOVER BEFORE 140 MPH POLICE CHASE

CHP issued a SigAlert shortly after 8 a.m. for the closure of lanes 4, 5 and 6 as crews worked to clear the wreckage.

Under CHP policy, SigAlerts are issued for unplanned events or circumstances that could delay a large number of motorists for at least 30 minutes. Traffic collisions, spilled loads, flooding and unexpected congestion are among the situations that can trigger an alert.

The agency extended the SigAlert for another 30 minutes at about 8:30 a.m.

The collision occurred on northbound I-405 near Santa Monica Boulevard in West Los Angeles. The freeway continues north from the Westwood area toward the Sepulveda Pass.

VEHICLE NARROWLY AVOIDS SLAMMING INTO DRIVER ON SIDE OF OHIO HIGHWAY, DRAMATIC VIDEO SHOWS

Caltrans has previously directed motorists seeking an alternate northbound route from Santa Monica Boulevard to travel east to Sepulveda Boulevard before continuing north to an I-405 entrance at Moraga Drive.

The lanes affected by Thursday morning’s crash were eventually cleared and reopened.

The cause of the crash was not immediately clear, and authorities had not announced whether any citations or arrests resulted from the collision.

Fox News Digital reached out to the California Highway Patrol for additional information but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Russia’s ‘Amazon’ in deep-strike Ukraine blitz, wiping billions from Putin-linked CEO
item.description: Ukraine's drone strikes have knocked out 27% of Wildberries warehouse capacity, with losses estimated up to $8.5 billion as Russia's logistics reels.
item.content:encoded:
Ukraine’s expanding deep-strike campaign impacted Russia’s largest online retailer again Thursday, when a drone struck an oil and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan, sparking a fire at a Wildberries facility, according to reports.

Wildberries, often described as "Russia’s Amazon," said the facility was evacuated and that no goods were being stored there at the time, Reuters reported.

The strike marked the latest in a series of Ukrainian attacks affecting the e-commerce firm's sites across Russia that began July 18, when drones hit centers in Kotovsk and Elektrostal, killing seven and wounding more than 60, according to reports.

BRINGING THE WAR TO PUTIN’S FRONT DOOR: IS UKRAINE’S ENERGY STRIKE STRATEGY WORKING?

Four days later, drones struck facilities in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk, sparking fires and injuring 15 people.

"We can call it ‘kinetic sanctions enforcement,’ or Ukraine’s adaptation of economic coercion into physical strikes," Kateryna Bondar, senior fellow at the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital.

"Kyiv’s goal is to steadily raise the cost and risk of sustaining Russia’s war economy," the former Ukrainian government advisor said, adding that the economic impact could be significant.

The total losses incurred by Wildberries and its sellers as a result of the attacks have been estimated at 600 billion to 800 billion rubles ($6 billion to $8.5 billion), Ukrainian media outlet Pravda reported.

"With only 5% to 7% of sellers insured, the damage is cascading onto tens of thousands of small businesses and forcing Russia’s logistics sector to reprice wartime risk," Bondar said.

"Roughly 27% of Wildberries warehouse capacity is reportedly out of operation," she added.

'PURE HELL' IN MOSCOW AS UKRAINIAN DRONES STRIKE MAJOR REFINERY SUPPLYING CAPITAL'S FUEL MARKET

Beyond the financial toll, Bondar said the strikes carry a significant psychological impact.

"I’ve listened to videos recorded by witnesses, and reactions range from fear, shock and anger to disappointment in the capabilities of Russian air defenses," she said. "So, that effect is clearly being achieved."

Wildberries founder and CEO Tatyana Kim has since accused Ukraine of deliberately targeting a civilian company. In a July 31 video address, she described the strikes as a "terrorist attack."

"For nearly two weeks now, our company's warehouses have been under terrorist attack. Why our warehouses, of all places? Attacks against us are attacks against hundreds of millions of people in 10 countries at once," Kim said.

Kim claimed Wildberries entrepreneurs in Russia and partner countries, including China and Kazakhstan, had "suffered losses amounting to billions," arguing that the company itself not be held responsible for covering all the losses.

MOSCOW, KYIV ASSASSINS HUNT WEAPONS BOSSES AS UKRAINE WAR SPILLS BEYOND THE BATTLEFIELD

"Merchants will start pricing Russian logistics risk into their business decisions," Bondar warned.

Kim said sellers from ten countries, including China, have suffered billions in losses, while Wildberries maintains it is not liable, which creates incentives to diversify away from the platform, shorten inventory cycles, demand prepayment and increase insurance costs.

Bondar said Kyiv views the retail giant’s sprawling supply chain through a military and economic lens.

"Kyiv assesses Wildberries warehouses as distribution nodes for dual-use goods, including body armor, helmets, fiber optic cable for FPV drones, and navigation components, as well as channels for sanctions circumvention," Bondar said.

"The strikes also retaliate for Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s civilian logistics infrastructure, including the Nova Poshta and Ukrposhta networks."

RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY

Kim is Russia’s richest woman, with Forbes estimating her fortune at roughly $7 billion in July.

"Kim matters to the Kremlin less as an individual than as an asset already absorbed into its clan system," Bondar said. "The current strikes expose the limits of her political protection. The Kremlin has remained largely silent, while Kim is negotiating tax deferrals rather than receiving compensation or air-defense protection from them.

"It sends the message to Russia’s business elite that proximity to power does not guarantee protection, and private businesses are expected to absorb the costs of war."

The attacks have also drawn scrutiny regarding Wildberries’ warehouse security procedures and a controversial new policy restricting workers’ cellphone use.

REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES

"The smartphone ban is officially justified as an air-defense security measure, but the real concern appears to be information control," Bondar said.

"Employees were filming strikes and sharing footage in real time, making the damage and the war’s impact on ordinary Russians impossible to hide," she added. "The policy also exposes a serious vulnerability. Workers reportedly had their phones locked away during attacks, limiting their ability to call for help.

"Wildberries cannot harden its sprawling warehouses or provide air defense, so it is controlling the one thing it can — what gets recorded and seen."

item.title: Stacey Abrams tells nodding Kamala Harris that southerners have lived under 'soft authoritarianism' since 1776
item.description: Stacey Abrams told Kamala Harris on her podcast that the American South represents what authoritarianism looks like in the U.S., dating back to 1776.
item.content:encoded:
Georgia Democrat Stacey Abrams suggested to a nodding former Vice President Kamala Harris during an interview Thursday that the American South is what the United States looks like as an authoritarian country.

On her "Assembly Required" podcast, Abrams, who ran unsuccessfully twice for governor of Georgia, spoke to Harris about the future of the Democratic Party and the challenges it faces, particularly in southern states.

"I grew up in Mississippi, came of age in Georgia, and I know you've been spending a lot of time in the South recently. You've been to Tennessee and Louisiana and North Carolina," Abrams told Harris. "And what I tell people when they want to understand what authoritarianism can look like in the U.S., I say, ‘Look South.’ We have lived under soft authoritarianism, I would say, since, oh, 1776."

"And what it has meant is that we have seen the warning signs long before the rest of the country, but we've also been the architects of the solutions long before the rest of the country understands it," she continued.

BLOCKBUSTER SUPREME COURT VOTING RIGHTS RULING IGNITES REDISTRICTING WAR ACROSS SOUTHERN STATES

She went on to claim that the American debate about voter ID is fake.

"And when you talk about what's happening in North Carolina, I liken it to the fact that we are having this false debate about voter ID. Every state requires that you identify who you are. But if you're in Texas, you can use your gun license and not your student ID," she said. "If you're in North Carolina, yeah, you can vote if you can manage to get to a polling place where, you know, a lot of students don't actually have cars. They don't have the ability to do so."

NewsBusters managing editor Curtis Houck skewered her comment.

SEN MARK WARNER CALLED OUT IN ABC INTERVIEW FOR INACCURATE VOTER ID CLAIMS

"Virginia has had voter ID for over a decade and had both Republicans and Democrats emerge victorious. It's an incredibly simple but important way to give voters peace of mind anytime they head to the polls," he told Fox News Digital.

Abrams has enjoyed highly favorable liberal media coverage in her career, which has included harsh criticism of Georgia's voting laws, advocacy for more progressive voting bills, and her refusal to officially concede her 2018 loss to Republican Brian Kemp. She lost more handily in 2022 in a rematch and conceded that race.

"The liberal, elitist media never fact-check these deranged assertions cloaked in historical references. If asking for an ID that must be scanned and recited to the poll worker is authoritarianism, then America stopped being a free country multiple lifetimes ago," Houck said.

Abrams' close loss to Kemp in 2018 was considered a major boon toward Georgia becoming a swing state that merited national Democratic investment.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Harris, who lost the 2024 presidential election, is considered a possible Democratic contender again in 2028. While Joe Biden won Georgia with her on the ticket in 2020 — ending a long Democratic presidential losing streak in the state — Harris lost Georgia to Donald Trump in 2024.

item.title: Resurfaced assault report puts Dem Senate nominee in GOP crosshairs: 'Graham Platner 2.0'
item.description: Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine, faces GOP attacks after a 1988 police report details a late-night brawl and assault claims.
item.content:encoded:
Republicans are targeting Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson after a newly resurfaced 1988 police record detailed accusations that he assaulted a man and pushed his longtime partner during a late-night confrontation in Fort Kent, Maine.

Jackson, a one-time logger and a former state Senate president, was chosen a couple of weeks ago by Maine Democrats to replace embattled oysterman Graham Platner, who won the June Democratic Senate nomination in a landslide before imploding and dropping out of the race last month amid rape allegations that he denied.

Jackson is challenging longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a high-stakes race that's among a dozen that will determine if the GOP holds onto its slim Senate majority.

MAINE DEMOCRATS CROWN TROY JACKSON AS PLATNER REPLACEMENT FACES INTENSE SCRUTINY

Collins is the only GOP incumbent running for re-election in a state President Donald Trump lost in the 2024 election. A Fox News poll in Maine released on Wednesday indicated Jackson holding a slight two-point edge over Collins, which was within the survey's sampling error.

"Troy Jackson is Graham Platner 2.0: Violent and unhinged," the Republican National Committee charged in a social media post.

Meanwhile, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, referring to Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, wrote on X, "Is this incredibly disturbing report of violence and abuse not enough for you to drop Troy Jackson?"

WHAT THE NEW FOX NEWS POLL IN MAINE'S CRUCIAL SENATE RACE SHOWS

The Bangor Daily News reported that the police report accused Jackson of assaulting another man during a late-night brawl on March 12, 1988.

The brawl was over Jackson's longtime partner Lana Pelletier, who, according to records, is also his second cousin. Jackson and Pelletier share two adult children.

The police report indicates that Pelletier told officers at the time that Jackson "pushed her around," a statement she now denies making.

According to the report, the then-19-year-old Jackson went to a home in Fort Kent, Maine around 2 a.m.

After the occupant of the house told Jackson to go away, the report says the future state lawmaker "kicked the door in" and grabbed his rival by the throat before punching him in the face, causing the victim’s glasses to leave a cut. The report added that a friend broke up the ensuing fight.

DEMOCRATS STAND BY JACKSON AFTER LATEST CONTROVERSY

Jackson said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital, "Nearly forty years ago, when I was 19 years old, I got into a fight with another man. I took responsibility for it then, and I take responsibility for it now."

"But let me be clear: I have never been violent with my partner Lana, or any other woman. This happened nearly four decades ago, and I assure Mainers this incident in no way reflects the man I am today or the life I've led in the years since," the Democratic Senate nominee added.

Pelletier told Fox News Digital in a statement, "I do not remember making the statements attributed to me and they are not accurate. This is the first time I have seen this report from 40 years ago. Troy and I have built a life and family together and I know the person he has been through the decades since, both as a caring partner and father."

"I understand Maine voters want to learn about Troy as he seeks to represent them but personal attacks on my family are unacceptable," she added. item.title: My son's ultrasound showed me the truth about abortion Massachusetts now denies
item.description: Gov. Maura Healey signed a law on Monday removing Massachusetts' 24-week abortion restrictions, replacing specific conditions with physician judgment alone.
item.content:encoded:
My son turned 1 year old last month, but I still have his ultrasound pictures up on the fridge. They were the first time I got to see his little hands, his feet, and even his eyes open wide and looking, somehow, right at me. He was 20 weeks along in that picture. Already kicking. Already reaching. Already becoming the boy who now pulls himself up on that same refrigerator door.

I thought of him — of those pictures curling on my fridge — as I watched Massachusetts Democrat Gov. Maura Healey sign a law this week that strips protections from every baby at the same stage of pregnancy against late-term abortion.

The state’s new law, the Prioritizing Patient Access to Care Act, guts existing legislation that restricted abortions at 24 weeks and later to cases involving the mother’s life, physical or mental health, or severe fetal diagnoses, and replaces those specific statutory conditions with a sweeping new standard stating that "an abortion may be performed by a physician based upon the professional judgment of the physician." No gestational limit. No requirement that any particular maternal or fetal condition be present.

DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

Surrounded by cheering supporters at the signing, Healey insisted the new law is meant to protect women. Protect them from what, exactly? Massachusetts women facing the truly horrific scenarios — pregnancies that turned fatal for mother or child — already had access to abortion under the state’s prior law. This bill doesn’t hand them a single protection they didn’t already have.

What it does do is remove the specific guardrails that governed abortions at such a late stage — namely, the requirement that a physician determine that the abortion was necessary to protect the mother’s life, physical or mental health, or was warranted because of a lethal or extraordinarily grave fetal diagnosis.

Under the new law, none of those circumstances have to be established in the statute. The legal standard is simply the physician’s professional judgment.

It’s worth pausing on what’s actually happening inside the womb at 24 weeks. Just like my son in his ultrasound pictures, babies at 24 weeks have a fully formed face, fingerprints, and a heartbeat that’s been audible for months. Their lungs are still maturing, but their inner ears are developed enough to hear voices, and they respond to sound and touch.

SURROGATE GIVES BIRTH IN TEXAS TO BABY WITH HEART DEFECT AFTER PARENTS REQUESTED ABORTION

This is also around the point in pregnancy known as viability — the gestational age at which, with intensive NICU care, a baby born prematurely has a real chance of survival outside the womb. My sister-in-law is a NICU nurse and has cared for several of these infants, some as young as 22 and 23 weeks old. She has watched their mothers sit through countless sleepless nights, praying for tiny lungs to grow strong enough and hearts to keep beating. It is a testament to modern medicine how often those prayers are answered.

So what, exactly, separates the baby fighting for his life in the NICU from the baby electively aborted at the very same stage — other than whether someone wanted him?

The truth at the center of the abortion debate — the one its advocates rarely reckon with — is that a person’s life has worth in and of itself, independent of anyone else’s readiness to receive it. My son had worth and meaning before I was ready for him, before I’d fully wrapped my mind around what it meant to be his mother. That worth was never mine to take away, and neither was his life.

Even those who generally support abortion during the very early stages of pregnancy know this to be true, which is why support for abortion restrictions climbs sharply once you move past the first trimester.

LATE-TERM ABORTION TAKES FRONT SEAT AS BLUE STATE RUSHES TO EXPAND ACCESS BEFORE SESSION ENDS

A Harvard-Harris poll found that 72% of Americans said abortion should be limited to 15 weeks or earlier, while another Harvard-Harris poll found that just 10% support allowing abortion through nine months.

In other words, Healey and the Massachusetts Democrats weren’t overriding some fringe position when they gutted the state’s restrictions; they were overriding the consensus. Theirs is the fringe position now, held by just nine other Democrat-run states, in addition to some of the most totalitarian countries in the world, such as China.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

You’d think that fact might give Democrats pause. Instead, Healey and the women surrounding her on Monday looked overjoyed — smiling, applauding, celebrating a policy that is, by any honest reckoning, both logically and morally indefensible.

This law does something else, too: it severs women from the very instincts that make motherhood what it is. As mothers, the question that motivates us, that gives us purpose, that reorders everything else in our lives around it, is: What do we owe the lives entrusted to us? We ask it at 2 a.m. with a crying newborn who can’t tell us what’s wrong. We ask it when they’re sick, when they’re struggling, when they need something we can’t yet name.

The answer, every time, is that we owe them unconditional love and care. That question doesn’t start at birth. It starts the moment we understand there is a life to answer for. And at 24 weeks — hell, much, much earlier than that — there is no honest way to pretend that moment hasn’t already come.

This law asks something different of women. It asks us to pretend the question doesn’t apply yet — to treat a baby at 24 weeks not as a life entrusted to us, but as a decision that ends the moment we stop wanting it to continue; and to treat the same instinct that governs a mother at 2 a.m. with her newborn as irrelevant three months earlier, as if a mother’s obligation has an on/off switch a doctor can flip.

It doesn’t. It never has. And no law, however cheerfully signed, can make that instinct go away. It can only ask women to ignore it.

item.title: Former Vikings captain Jack Brewer reacts to Abdul El-Sayed's Senate primary victory in Michigan
item.description: Jack Brewer calls Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate primary win a "warning shot to America" and backs Michele Tafoya to flip Minnesota blue voters.
item.content:encoded:
Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brewer described Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary as a "warning shot to America," while praising Michele Tafoya as a credible conservative capable of winning over Minnesota Democrats and independent voters.

"It’s good when you see the darkness before you," Brewer said when asked about El-Sayed. "You see exactly what we’re up against as Americans when we have our major cities, major states, with folks like this winning primaries on the verge of having control of populations of that size.

"I mean, it’s scary, man," he continued. "It should be a warning shot to America, a warning shot of really where our country is."

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Brewer said President Donald Trump’s election victory did not eliminate the political and cultural problems he sees across the country.

"When President Trump won the election, it didn’t fix everything," he said. "We’ve got a lot, lot of things to fix. And it’s pretty scary when you start to see these radical leftists starting to gain more and more power across the country."

El-Sayed, a physician and former Detroit public health director, narrowly defeated U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. He will face Republican Mike Rogers in November.

El-Sayed ran on a progressive platform that includes Medicare-for-all, higher taxes on billionaire wealth, campaign finance reform and an end to unconditional U.S. military aid to Israel.

Brewer acknowledged he had not closely followed El-Sayed before the primary campaign entered its final stages.

"Man, I didn’t know much about him to be honest with you," Brewer said. "As the election became closer and closer, you started to hear and see stories and hear the things that he says."

Brewer did not identify a particular El-Sayed policy or statement that concerned him.

"All I can think about is radical, right? And confused," Brewer said. "It just seems like everything that comes out of his mouth is confusion.

"If he’s speaking confusion, that means we have a voting populace that’s confused themselves to be following a guy like this."

El-Sayed’s victory occurred in Michigan, not Minnesota. He is not running against Tafoya. The two races were discussed together as examples of the broader national battle between progressive and conservative candidates in the 2026 midterms.

On another note, Brewer was happy to see Michele Tafoya’s victory in Minnesota’s Republican U.S. Senate primary.

"I was very happy," he said. "Michele Tafoya, who’s a friend and someone that I highly, highly respect, it’s good to see grounded conservative voices stepping up in that state."

Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter, won the Republican primary with 52.07% of the vote. Former Navy SEAL Adam Schwarze finished second with 23.96%, while former NBA player Royce White placed third with 11.15%, according to unofficial results from the Minnesota secretary of state.

Tafoya will face Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who defeated U.S. Rep. Angie Craig in the DFL primary.

"To see someone like herself, and someone that has a name and credibility, is important, especially being a Republican," Brewer said. "You have the cards stacked against you in a lot of ways in a state like Minnesota."

No Republican has won a statewide election in Minnesota since 2006. Kamala Harris carried the state in the 2024 presidential election with 50.92% of the vote, compared with Trump’s 46.68%.

Despite that history, Brewer predicted Tafoya could build a coalition extending beyond the Republican base.

"I think she has a chance to bring over enough Democratic voters and independents to win that election," he said. "So, I’m praying for her."

Former NBA player Royce White, who unsuccessfully challenged Tafoya in the Republican primary, also recently announced his plans to declare for the 2027 WNBA Draft.

Brewer said he had met White several times and respected his effort to challenge the WNBA’s approach to transgender eligibility.

THE WNBA HAS LIMITED OPTIONS AFTER TWO MEN DECLARED FOR THE DRAFT, AND THOSE OPTIONS AREN'T GREAT

"I’ve met Royce on a couple occasions," Brewer said. "A lot of respect for him."

White and former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom have announced plans to seek entry into the 2027 WNBA Draft. Their announcements are intended to test — or protest —t he league’s eligibility rules by claiming that they identify as women for professional basketball purposes.

"I think what he’s doing and Enes is doing is they’re trying to stand up for women," Brewer said.

The league has not declared White or Freedom eligible. It said this week there were "no immediate eligibility matters" affecting the WNBA and denounced what it called bad-faith attempts to use the subject to demean or marginalize others.

The WNBA has not adopted a publicly available policy saying that surgery qualifies an athlete for the league. Medical organizations also note that transgender identity does not require surgery and that many transgender people never seek surgical treatment.

Asked what he would tell Vikings fans before the midterm elections, Brewer urged them to reject Minnesota’s current political leadership.

"Stop supporting foolishness," he said. "Enough is enough."

Brewer pointed to his own history in the state. He attended the University of Minnesota before playing for the Vikings and three other NFL teams.

"I lived in Minnesota for a long time," he said. "I grew up a Vikings fan before I even got a chance to go play there. I went to the University of Minnesota, some of the greatest years of my life.

"People have common sense in Minnesota," Brewer continued. "My message to Minnesota is use the common sense that you have.

"Stop letting these people that have mental health issues represent you," he said. "You have people that are psychologically not there, and you’re allowing them to represent the state of Minnesota."

Brewer did not identify which officeholders he meant or provide evidence supporting that characterization.

At the same time, he praised Vikings fans as some of the most welcoming people he encountered during his professional football career.

"I played for four NFL teams, and there is nothing like a Minnesota Vikings fan," Brewer said. "These people will have you at home at their dinner table. They will cook for you. They’re the most hospitable people in the world, the nicest, most purest people in the world.

"And right now they’re being made a mockery of by the woke left," he added. "I wouldn’t even call them progressive, because they’re not progressive. There’s nothing about progress associated with these leftists. They’ve lost their minds."

Brewer is a prominent Trump ally. He serves as chair of Opportunity Now and vice chair of the Center for 1776 at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative organization closely aligned with the Trump administration.

item.title: Piker demands Democrats defend him from attacks, claims he’s no ‘toxic radical force'
item.description: Hasan Piker demanded Democrats defend him during a livestream as Republican criticism of his rhetoric becomes a flashpoint in key midterm races.
item.content:encoded:
Far-left streamer Hasan Piker called on Democratic Party leaders during a Wednesday livestream to defend him and accept his place in their coalition as Republican criticism of his rhetoric emerged as an issue in key midterm races, while a former staffer for former President Joe Biden told Fox News Digital on Thursday that candidates should disavow Piker and refocus on local issues.

During the livestream, Piker declared himself part of the Democratic coalition and said Republicans were using criticism of him to distract from what he described as the "cost-of-living crisis."

"Democrats, listen to me, I know we don't always see eye to eye on a lot of stuff, but you have to literally, at some point — I know you don't want to do this — defend me," he said. 

"Not because you love what I have to say, not because I'm part of this coalition, even though I am, whether you like it or not, but you are going to inevitably have to say, ‘This is a ridiculous conversation that we're having because the real conversation Republicans don't want to have is the cost-of-living crisis,’" Piker continued.

DAVID MARCUS: WHY IT'S TOO LATE FOR DEMS TO DITCH PIKER AND HIS AMERICA-HATING SOCIALISM

He then urged Democrats to accept a political setback in order to challenge how critics portray him.

"That requires you to basically to take the L a little bit and maybe be a bit more honest about how I'm not this dangerous, toxic radical force," Piker said.

"Democrats don’t have to adopt every influencer who happens to support some Dem candidates," moderate Democratic strategist Yemisi Egbewole told Fox News Digital. "I don’t understand why they would waste their political capital on it either. Hasan is perfectly capable of defending himself."

Egbewole, former chief of staff to the Biden White House Press Office, said embracing Piker would keep him at the center of the party's political debate.

"Don’t embrace him, and he erases himself from the conversation," she added.

HASAN PIKER'S DEFENSE OF HAMAS HAVING 'RIGHT TO RESIST MILITARILY' DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS

The dispute is playing out in two battleground states. Piker campaigned with Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed before he narrowly defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., and rallied with Michigan gubernatorial candidate and Democratic Socialists of America member Francesca Hong before David Crowley defeated her in the Wisconsin Democratic primary Tuesday. Piker previously called for Democrats who opposed El-Sayed to face punishment.

Crowley ruled out campaigning with Piker while seeking to unite Democrats against Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany, according to an "UpFront" clip posted Thursday.

"No, I don't plan on campaigning with Hasan," Crowley said, adding, "I don't want to lend credibility to platforms that I believe further divides us."

Piker responded to Crowley on X by wishing him success against Tiffany and urging the Democratic nominee to consider policies that Piker credited with driving primary turnout.

"This is devastating news for me, i however wish crowley the best of luck for the wisconsin trifecta. hope he takes some of the great policies that brought out 300k wisconsinites into consideration as the dems work to defeat tom tiffany as a unified front!" Piker wrote.

WISCONSIN DEMOCRATIC CANDIDATE FOR GOVERNOR DAVID CROWLEY REVEALS HE WON'T CAMPAIGN WITH HASAN PIKER

Algemeiner Washington correspondent Corey Walker rejected Piker’s appeal and cited the streamer’s treatment of ideological opponents.

"Nobody owes you a single thing. Hasan Piker and his fanbase are relentlessly brutal towards anyone they have the slightest disagreement with," Walker said.

"Piker will mock, smear, defame and ruthlessly target his ideological adversaries. He deserves the same level of sympathy and support he gives everyone else: zero," he added.

Freelance journalist Magdi Jacobs said disavowal was the clearest way for Democrats to end the controversy surrounding Piker.

"If Democrats want the conversation to not be about Hasan Piker, the logical path is to disavow Hasan Piker," Jacobs said. "If they embrace Hasan Piker, the conversation about Hasan Piker will continue."

Fox News Digital reached out to Piker and the DNC for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: Beach walk takes horrifying turn after woman spots something scattered in the sand
item.description: Nearly 30 dead dogfish sharks washed up on a Jersey Shore beach, and a shark ecologist reveals thoughts on what likely caused the rare mass stranding event.
item.content:encoded:
A morning stroll along a portion of the Jersey Shore took an alarming turn when a woman discovered nearly 30 dead sharks scattered across a popular beach.

The sharks, which have been identified as juvenile dogfish, were recently found in Sea Isle City, New Jersey, roughly 20 miles north of Cape May.

The discovery of so many sharks at once is a rare occurrence, shark ecologist Mike Heithaus told Fox News Digital.

TEXAS TEEN BITTEN BY BARRACUDA IN POPULAR VACATION SPOT AFTER BRACELET GLINTS IN WATER

"This is definitely something that's pretty rare, to see that many sharks washed up on the beach," said Heithaus, dean of Florida International University's College of Arts, Sciences & Education. 

The beachgoer, Michelle Greenling, told CBS Philadelphia she found 29 dead sharks between 29th and 39th streets along the shore.

"The first couple weren't too surprising, but when I saw three and four and five, I knew something was up," Greenling said.

The beachgoer described the sight as "definitely concerning."

BOY STUMBLES ON STRANGE BEACH OBJECT IDENTIFIED AS RARE 1.8M-YEAR-OLD FOSSIL

"I was concerned about the water. I was concerned about the sharks," she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Greenling for further comment.

Heithaus told Fox News Digital that dogfish gather in large schools, meaning a group could have been affected by the same event.

While a toxin might initially appear to be one possible explanation, he said he would expect other marine species to have been affected as well.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"The fact that there aren't lots of other different kinds of animals washing up at the same time suggests it's not some kind of pollution or toxin in the environment," said Heithaus, who was not involved in the discovery or analysis.

"If I had to make a guess, probably something happened to them, and they were caught, but [they] weren't what people were looking for, and so they got discarded."

Heithaus said scientists are increasingly using monitoring buoys and other systems as coastal oceans change, allowing researchers to track conditions and identify potential threats.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"We've learned enough that we can monitor water quality and figure out what's going on ahead of these events happening so we can make interventions when we might have to," he said.

"But, you know, in this case, it looks like it was probably something else."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Heithaus also advised beachgoers who encounter large numbers of dead marine animals to alert local authorities or wildlife officials.

Dogfish typically have a lifespan of 35 to 40 years, according to NOAA Fisheries' website.

"Like all sharks, dogfish grow slowly, mature late in life and live a long time," the site states.

item.title: Jon Rahm's reported exit from LIV Golf would pose devastation to breakaway circuit amid uncertainties
item.description: LIV Golf sources say they are almost resigned to Jon Rahm departing the league, a move that could devastate the circuit's future investor plans.
item.content:encoded:
Among the infinite number of questions surrounding LIV Golf and its future, the most intriguing and perhaps most important involves which players choose to stay on board and which look to bolt amid the current state of total uncertainty.

A new report suggests we may get an answer from Jon Rahm – one of the few stars remaining on LIV – sooner rather than later, and the reported answer would be disastrous for the breakaway circuit.

The Telegraph's James Corrigan reported Thursday that the belief within LIV is that Rahm will soon quit the league. The report stated that "LIV sources have indicated that they are almost resigned to Rahm departing."

LIV GOLF CEO QUIETS SPECULATION WITH ANNOUNCEMENT OF NEW INVESTOR TO KEEP CIRCUIT AFLOAT INTO 2027

One does not have to understand the inner workings of LIV Golf, have access to its financials or know every detail there is to know about the new, unnamed investor the league announced for 2027 to understand that a Rahm departure would be devastating.

Rahm, a two-time major champion, leaving LIV Golf wouldn't be a direct comparison to Caitlin Clark leaving the WNBA to play in another league, but it wouldn't be that far off given the circumstances. Bryson DeChambeau leaving LIV Golf would have the same effect as Clark leaving the WNBA.

Any potential investors, including the one LIV CEO Scott O'Neil announced earlier this month, will not be motivated to hand over millions of dollars if one of the biggest stars in the sport isn't a part of the circuit. O'Neil explained that a "term sheet" had been signed by the unknown investor and was hopeful a concrete agreement would be announced in September.

Rahm has two years remaining on his current contract, but the Telegraph, among other outlets, has reported he is still due a nine-figure check of the $300 million signing bonus he signed to join the circuit.

The Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced earlier this year that it was ceasing its funding of LIV Golf at the conclusion of the 2026 season, which may make Rahm receiving what he is presumably owed a complicated endeavor.

Among the many wrinkles in the ongoing and unknown situation involving LIV Golf is the DP World Tour, which granted conditional releases to some LIV players this season so they could compete on both circuits.

The Athletic's Gabby Herzig reported Thursday that those conditional releases being offered in 2027 are "highly unlikely," which would force the hands of Rahm and others to decide if they want to compete on LIV or the DP World Tour.

Whether or not the PGA Tour offers a direct and immediate path for LIV players who opt to leave following the conclusion of the 2026 season is unknown. Past champion categories and major winners, like Rahm, retain some exemptions on Tour, although given how unprecedented the present is and future may be, it's unclear what pathway back would look like.

A Rahm departure from LIV coupled with DeChambeau opting to leave and focus on his YouTube channel, which is something he's mentioned multiple times, wouldn't hurt the future of LIV Golf; it would end it.

item.title: Anthony Volpe has face-palm moment with ABS system as first batter of minor league game
item.description: Anthony Volpe burned both ABS challenges in his first at-bat with Triple-A Scranton, losing on two strike calls after seeing three straight balls.
item.content:encoded:
Anthony Volpe is in a grind to get back to the big leagues, and his ABS performance Wednesday won't help his cause.

The New York Yankees sent the shortstop to the minor leagues earlier this month to bring up top shortstop prospect George Lombard Jr. because Volpe has never quite hit the ground running as a former top prospect himself.

Despite his struggles, Volpe had actually induced a healthy walk rate in his time with the big league club this season, but one would not think that given his first at-bat with Triple-A Scranton Wednesday.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Volpe saw three straight balls to begin the game and then took what he thought was ball four. It was called a strike, but Volpe challenged the call in hopes of getting on first base.

He was wrong.

The next pitch was an off-speed pitch that looked much more out of the zone than the previous pitch. But, given what had just occurred, he did not want to take the risk of losing both challenges at the start of the game.

Well, that's exactly what he did on the next pitch. He challenged strike three and was wrong again.

So, the team was out of challenges after just one batter.

He made up for it with a triple later on in the night, but it was not enough in the RailRiders' 11-3 loss to the Lehigh Valley IronPigs.

ALEX RODRIGUEZ DEFENDS DODGERS' SPENDING SPREE AS LIKELY LOCKOUT GETS CLOSER: 'I THINK IT'S GREAT'

Volpe has hit well since being demoted, hitting .304 (7-for-23) with a double, triple and homer. He has recorded at least one hit in each of his five games since being sent down.

In the majors this year, he was hitting .240 with a career-high .325 on-base percentage, but his .322 slugging percentage was the worst of his career. He had hit just one home run in 56 games.

Lombard, meanwhile, is hitting .320 with a .953 OPS in his first seven games as a major leaguer and had the exact opposite ABS fate as Volpe a couple of nights ago, correctly challenging two strike-three calls to draw a walk.

Volpe has been working at second base since being sent to the minors, perhaps showing the Yankees' hand for his future with the team.

item.title: Trump to rally with New York police in highlighting historic coast-to-coast violent crime drop
item.description: President Donald Trump travels to Nassau County Police Academy with Todd Blanche and Kash Patel to rally with cops and tout historic crime drop.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: President Donald Trump will travel with top federal law enforcement brass to Nassau County, New York, on Friday to rally with local police and tout what his office describes as a historic drop in violent crime nationwide, Fox News Digital has learned.

Trump, along with newly-confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, are scheduled to host the event at the Nassau County Police Academy, a top-notch 89,000-square-foot advanced training and intelligence center for police on Long Island.

While there, the 47th president is expected to give a rundown on the largest year-to-year decrease in violent crime since the FBI began recording crime statistics in 1936.

FBI REPORTS LARGEST DROP IN VIOLENT CRIME AND MURDER SINCE 1937 AS HOMICIDES FALL MORE THAN 18%

He plans to tout an estimated 18.1% drop in murder and non-negligent manslaughter, an 18.5% drop in robberies, a 7.6% decrease in rapes and a 7.2% decline in aggravated assault in 2025.

Further, Trump will announce that burglaries dropped by an estimated 15.8%, while larceny decreased by 9.8% and motor vehicle theft declined by 22.7%.

The statistics come from the FBI’s soon-to-be released 2025 Crime Statistics Report. Trump is expected to highlight for the officers his law and order policies that he says have led to safer neighborhoods and fewer crime victims.

TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS

"President Trump will visit the Nassau County Police Academy to do a rally with cops. President Trump promised to make America safe again and the data proves he has done just that," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

"Unlike Defund-the-Police Democrats, President Trump will always stand with our law enforcement officers and deliver safer American neighborhoods," she added, noting the far-left movement's push to get rid of law enforcement entirely.

It's been a banner week for the Trump administration in the way of successful crime reduction announcements.

Tuesday marked one year since Trump's bold deployment of the National Guard to Washington, D.C. in an effort to curb lawlessness in the nation's capital, dubbed the Safe and Beautiful initiative.

Patel said that D.C. is safer than it has been in decades thanks to the deployment and a surge of federal authorities in the city.

KASH PATEL TOUTS FBI 'FULL-THROTTLE MISSION' AFTER OPERATION SPRING CLEANING YIELDS 615 INDICTMENTS/COMPLAINTS

"Last summer, President Trump made the historic decision to surge federal resources to Washington D.C. to crack down on crime – and thanks to his brilliant leadership, the work of brave FBI agents and our law enforcement partners, and the support of our Justice Department, our nation’s capital is now safer than it’s been in decades," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital.

He said that the FBI, in conjunction with law enforcement partners, made 6,000 arrests, nearly 2,000 drug seizures and over 1,300 illegal firearm seizures over the year-long span.

The federal resources will remain in D.C. for the foreseeable future, Patel said.

"The greatest country on earth should have a capital city reflecting it — where American taxpayers can live, visit, and petition their government without fear of violent crime."

item.title: Dan Aykroyd details 'medieval times' reality of California while praising life in Canada
item.description: Dan Aykroyd described driving through Santa Monica's beauty alongside 60,000 homeless people, saying we are living in "frankly medieval times."
item.content:encoded:
Dan Aykroyd praised his Canadian roots while pondering world atrocities in a recently unearthed podcast.

Aykroyd, 74, admitted in a resurfaced clip from "The Adam Carolla Show" that he "loved going around the world," boasting that his Crystal Head Vodka was "made in Canada" where he was born – a place he believed to have a stark contrast to life in California.

"It's great to be living in the western world," he said before singing an old blues song with lyrics including, "Oh, this world is in an uproar, things all going wrong. The way the reds is cutting up, we ain't going to be here long."

DAN AYKROYD SURVIVED 50-FOOT FALL, CREDITS 'DIVINE INTERVENTION' FOR SAVING HIS LIFE

The "Ghostbusters" actor recalled a visit with a friend from Israel who stayed on his farm and once asked, "Dan, what is it like to live in a land where there's no war?"

"Here I am driving through the bucolic countryside ... and we're in Canada," he said. "We're driving to the drugstore to get an ice cream, and he tells me, 'What it is like to live in a country without war?' I thought to myself, ‘Boy, do I take things for granted, you know, around this place.’"

After Carolla reminisced on failed promises for the future, Aykroyd insisted there were "pockets of the world that are at peace and that there is harmony, you know, Santa Monica, California – harmony, peace, joy by the sea."

"It's beautiful there, beautiful houses and beautiful shops and lovely wide boulevards and 60,000 homeless," he said. "So the underside and the overside will always, always be there."

"We're living in frankly medieval times. You go, I drive very carefully in the car. I don't drive prison hours at night, have a gated place to live ... lock up at night. Bring my family close, whereas really I would like to take my family and let them run in the park at 1 in the morning."
